passage:
Monday: After the evening prayer, Nani notices nine-year-old Hafsa on the next mat, murmuring the same words half a beat behind, copying even the way Nani lowers her forehead. Nani says nothing, but folds her mat very slowly.
Thursday: Hafsa spills a glass of milk and says, 'Sabr, sabr,' exactly in Nani's tone. Nani laughs out loud.
Sunday: Hafsa's friend Lakshmi visits, and Hafsa retells Nani's story of the thirsty crow and the pot, word for word, even the pause before the ending. Lakshmi begs for another. That night Nani tells Hafsa's Ammi, 'They listen, you know. All of it stays.'

qa.q: Which story did Hafsa retell to Lakshmi?
qa.a: Nani's story of the thirsty crow and the pot.

qa.q: What was Nani feeling when she said, 'They listen, you know. All of it stays'?
qa.a: Nani felt moved and proud, sensing that her prayers, sayings and stories really matter in Hafsa's life.

qa.q: What could Hafsa's Ammi do to keep this learning going?
qa.a: Make time for Hafsa to sit with Nani for prayers and stories, and perhaps ask Nani to share a new saying now and then.

qa.q: How does Hafsa seem to see Nani's words and stories?
qa.a: Hafsa seems to treasure them, repeating Nani's sayings in the same tone and proudly passing the story on to Lakshmi.

grounding: Shows a grandmother noticing a grandchild copy her prayers, sayings and stories through daily contact, and feeling that her role has meaning.

passage: Gurleen, you asked how your baby will ever learn Punjabi here, with both grandmothers so far away. Let your Aparna Dida tell you something. When my son's family lived with me in Kolkata, I said my evening prayers aloud and told stories while shelling peas. I thought nobody listened. Then one afternoon I heard my grandson Tuhin, nine, telling his little sister, 'Slowly, slowly, the river fills the sea,' in my exact sing-song, finger raised like mine. Another day he corrected his father's Bangla. I sat on the steps and cried a little, happy. Nobody had given me that job. It came from simply being there every day.

qa.q: What saying did Tuhin tell his little sister?
qa.a: 'Slowly, slowly, the river fills the sea.'

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when she sat on the steps and cried a little?
qa.a: Aparna felt happy and moved, realising her prayers, stories and sayings had been passing to Tuhin just through everyday life.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed how Aparna saw the daily prayers and stories, and why?
qa.a: Hearing Tuhin repeat her saying in her exact sing-song; it showed that simply being present every day was already teaching him.

qa.q: How might Tuhin have seen Aparna's everyday stories at the time?
qa.a: To Tuhin they were probably just part of home, so natural that he copied them, gesture and all, without thinking of them as lessons.

grounding: Illustrates a grandmother who notices a grandchild copying her sayings, prayers and stories through daily contact and feels her role has meaning.

passage:
The power went out just as Aaji lit the evening lamp in the Nagpur flat, and her reading glasses were lost somewhere on the dark sofa. She fumbled for the prayer book, sighing.

Then Sunaina, nine, began the aarti from memory, word for word, the way Aaji sang it: slow on the second line, quick on the last. Her cousin Pallavi, seven, joined in, clapping on the beat.

Aaji stopped hunting for her glasses and just listened.

Afterwards, when Pallavi stubbed her toe on the doorframe, she said, exactly in Aaji's voice, "Arre, the door didn't move, you did!"

Aaji laughed so hard in the dark that she had to sit down. So it had all gone in.

qa.q: How old is Pallavi?
qa.a: Pallavi is seven.

qa.q: What was Aaji feeling as she listened in the dark?
qa.a: Aaji felt moved and delighted, seeing that her prayers and sayings had quietly gone into the children.

qa.q: How could the family keep this learning going once the lights are back?
qa.a: Let the girls lead the aarti some evenings and ask Aaji for more stories and sayings, so the passing-on stays daily.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sunaina to lead the aarti from memory?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel proud and grown-up, stepping in when Aaji couldn't read.

grounding: Shows a grandmother noticing, during a power cut, that her granddaughters have absorbed her prayers and sayings through daily contact.

passage:
Every afternoon from three to six, Kalyani minded her grandson Farhan in her Secunderabad flat while his parents worked. She told him old stories while she chopped vegetables, stories full of Telugu sayings he pretended not to hear.

On Thursday his school friend came over and bragged about a new cycle. From the stove, Kalyani heard Farhan say, "Don't show off, ra. Empty pots make the most noise," and then, in careful Telugu, the proverb itself.

Kalyani's spoon stopped. That was her line, her tone, even her little tilt of the head.

That evening, when her daughter came to collect him, Kalyani told the story twice.

qa.q: When does Kalyani mind Farhan?
qa.a: Kalyani minded Farhan every afternoon from three to six.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani tell the story twice to her daughter?
qa.a: She was proud and delighted; hearing her own proverb, tone and head tilt from Farhan made her afternoons feel meaningful.

qa.q: How could Farhan's parents build on what Kalyani is passing on?
qa.a: Ask Farhan to share Kalyani's stories and sayings at home, and keep the afternoons with her, since daily contact is what taught him.

qa.q: How might Farhan see the stories he 'pretended not to hear'?
qa.a: Farhan may think of them as background chatter, not noticing how much he has absorbed until the words come out of his own mouth.

grounding: Illustrates a grandmother noticing her grandson using her sayings and language, passed on through everyday afternoons together.

passage:
"Once upon a time, in a village with no water," Yamini began, torch under her chin, "there lived a very, very thirsty crow."
"Like Dadi's story?" Gargi whispered from the bottom bunk.
"Shh. Listen. 'Beta, patience fills the pot,' the crow said to itself."
In the corridor, Dadi stopped with the milk glasses.
"That's what Dadi says!" said Gargi.
"I know. And then the crow drops pebbles, one by one, and never gives up."
Dadi came in, set down the glasses and sat on the edge of the bunk. "And who taught you that?"
"You did, Dadi," Yamini said, as if it were obvious. "Every night."
Dadi smoothed Yamini's hair and said nothing for a moment, eyes shining.

qa.q: What saying does the crow use in Yamini's story?
qa.a: The crow said, 'Beta, patience fills the pot.'

qa.q: What was Dadi feeling as she sat on the bunk with shining eyes?
qa.a: Dadi felt touched and proud, hearing her own story and saying come back in Yamini's voice.

qa.q: What could Dadi do to keep this going?
qa.a: Invite Yamini to tell a story some nights and explain the sayings behind them to both girls, so the passing-on runs both ways.

qa.q: How does Yamini see Dadi's stories?
qa.a: To Yamini they are simply part of every night, so obvious that she's surprised Dadi even asks where she learned it.

grounding: Shows a grandmother overhearing a grandchild retell her bedtime story and saying word for word, and feeling her role matters.

passage: Last winter I noticed something that still makes me smile. I am Dilnaz, Mamaiji, grandmother of four, and I live with my son's family in Mumbai. Every morning I tie my kusti and say my prayers by the window. One day my granddaughter Kavitha, nine, stood beside me with a ribbon round her waist, moving her lips like me. Her mother is a Hindu from Pune, and Kavitha goes to the temple with her too. But she had learnt my words, just by watching. Later she scolded her brother with my saying: "Good thoughts, good words, good deeds, Rustom!" I laughed so hard. My friends in small flats have to phone their grandchildren. Mine hear me every day. I felt useful again.

qa.q: What did Kavitha tie round her waist?
qa.a: A ribbon.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel on seeing Kavitha copy her prayers?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt delighted and useful again, as if her role had meaning.

qa.q: What does living together give this family that others may have to seek out?
qa.a: Daily contact lets Kavitha pick up Dilnaz's prayers and sayings naturally, while grandparents in separate homes may need phone calls or planned visits.

qa.q: How might Kavitha see her grandmother's morning prayers?
qa.a: Kavitha probably finds them interesting and special, a part of her day she wants to join in, alongside the temple visits with her mother.

grounding: It illustrates a grandmother who notices a grandchild copying her prayers and sayings and feels her role has meaning.
